principles.name: Exceptional client service
principles.description: Put the client's best interests first, make it easy to do business with the firm, and choose long-term relationships over short-term gain.
evidence_signals: Names the client or internal user affected and what they needed
Made a decision close to the client instead of escalating everything
Chose the durable fix over a quick win that would hurt clients later

principles.name: Operational excellence
principles.description: Set high standards, execute with discipline and urgency, manage risk and keep strong controls, and spend the firm's resources like an owner.
evidence_signals: Describes testing, change control or monitoring that kept a release safe
Quantifies the result with metrics or a scorecard
Cut waste or simplified a system and shows the saving
Follows through to completion, not just the design

principles.name: A commitment to integrity, fairness and responsibility
principles.description: Do the right thing even when it is hard, follow the letter and spirit of rules, face facts, admit mistakes and learn from them.
evidence_signals: Admits a mistake plainly and describes how it was surfaced and fixed
Raised a risk or compliance concern rather than working around it
Uses one consistent version of the facts with stakeholders

principles.name: A great team and winning culture
principles.description: Build strong, diverse teams, communicate openly with direct feedback, support colleagues and challenge the status quo responsibly.
evidence_signals: Gave or received direct feedback and acted on it
Helped a teammate or new joiner succeed
Challenged an existing process with a better proposal and got buy-in

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Two easy-to-medium coding problems, sometimes with aptitude questions. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: HireVue video interview
rounds.notes: Mainly for students and new grads: preset behavioral prompts with short prep time and a fixed recording window. Some interns go through the Code for Good hackathon instead of a Superday.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: One or two medium problems in a shared editor plus a resume project discussion; Java teams may ask language internals. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Superday coding and code review
rounds.notes: A medium coding problem and a short pull-request review exercise (bugs, style, missing tests). Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Superday system design
rounds.notes: Above entry level. Banking-grade prompts: idempotent and auditable payments, end-of-day reconciliation, rate limiters, market-data fan-out. Stress on consistency, retries and proving correctness to an auditor.

rounds.name: Superday behavioral
rounds.notes: Teamwork, production incidents, change control and integrity. Many Superday rounds mix technical and behavioral questions.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: For experienced hires: past scope, motivation for JPMorganChase and team fit.

rounds.name: Online assessment or HireVue
rounds.notes: Maths, logic and programming test, or recorded screening questions. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.notes: SQL and Python problems. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML and statistics
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior data scientist or ML engineer
rounds.notes: ML theory (bagging versus boosting, regularization, imbalanced data), probability such as Bayes' theorem, and a deep dive into a resume ML project.

rounds.name: Behavioral and fit
rounds.notes: Why JPMorganChase, stakeholder work and experience-based questions.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background and interest. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Past experience and role fit; products launched end to end.

rounds.name: Team interviews
rounds.notes: Stakeholder management, a challenging project, what product management means, product manager versus product owner.

rounds.name: Product case
rounds.notes: Reported only for some teams: improving a banking or payments product within risk and regulatory limits.

question_patterns.pattern: A situation where the right thing and the convenient thing differed, such as a control or compliance concern
values: A commitment to integrity, fairness and responsibility

question_patterns.pattern: Working with many teams or stakeholders to deliver something, including a disagreement
values: A great team and winning culture

question_patterns.pattern: Why technology at a bank, and why this firm and line of business

values: A commitment to integrity, fairness and responsibility

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time something you shipped broke in production. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real incident with meaningful impact. Explain how it was detected, how you contained it (rollback, feature flag), who you informed and when, and the honest root cause. Finish with the lasting fix: a test, a monitoring alert or a change-control step, and what you learned. Pitfalls: claiming you never broke anything, blaming another team, or no prevention step.
values: A commitment to integrity, fairness and responsibility

strong_signals: Contained fast and told people early

sample_questions.question: A release you worked on is showing some customers the wrong account balance. Walk me through what you would do.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Stay calm and process-driven: confirm and size the problem, stop the bleeding (roll back or disable the feature), escalate through the incident process, and tell operations and client-facing teams so customers get accurate information. Preserve evidence, find the root cause, correct affected records with an audit trail, and add controls to prevent repeats. Show you put client trust and accuracy ahead of speed.
values: A commitment to integrity, fairness and responsibility

strong_signals: Fixes records with an audit trail
watch_outs: Jumping to code changes before containing

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to work in technology at JPMorganChase rather than at a tech company?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show you understand the scale and impact: technology that moves trillions of dollars, serves millions of customers and must be secure and reliable. Name the line of business or platform that interests you and connect it to your experience. Mention the appeal of hard constraints such as regulation and correctness. Pitfalls: generic 'big brand' answers, or treating the bank as a fallback.

strong_signals: Names a line of business or platform

sample_questions.question: Design a payments backend that processes transfers exactly once and can be audited later.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify volume and consistency needs. Use idempotency keys on requests, a double-entry ledger as the source of truth, state machines for payment status, and an outbox or durable queue for downstream events. Cover retries with backoff, timeouts with unknown outcomes, reconciliation against external systems, immutable audit logs and access controls. Explain how you would prove to an auditor that no payment was lost or duplicated.
values: A commitment to integrity, fairness and responsibility

sample_questions.question: How would you design an end-of-day reconciliation job that matches the firm's trade records against a counterparty's?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define inputs, matching keys and tolerances, then a batch pipeline that normalizes both sides, matches exact and fuzzy records, and produces breaks for operations to investigate. Discuss scale and deadlines, reruns that must give the same result, late files, data lineage, and alerting when breaks exceed a threshold. Mention controls such as maker-checker for manual fixes.

watch_outs: No handling of late or missing files

sample_questions.question: Explain the difference between bagging and boosting, and how you would handle a heavily imbalanced fraud data set.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Bagging trains models on bootstrap samples in parallel to cut variance; boosting trains sequentially on previous errors to cut bias but can overfit. For imbalance: pick metrics such as precision-recall and cost-weighted loss instead of accuracy, use class weights or resampling, set thresholds by business cost, and validate on a time-based split to avoid leakage. Mention monitoring for drift as fraud patterns change.

sample_questions.question: How do you manage stakeholders with conflicting priorities on a product you own?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Use one concrete example. Show how you mapped stakeholders (business, technology, risk, compliance), made the trade-offs visible with data and client impact, agreed a decision process, and communicated the outcome to those who did not get their way. End with the result and how relationships held up.
values: A great team and winning culture

looking_for: Stakeholder management in a large firm

sample_questions.question: What is the difference between a product manager and a product owner, and which have you been?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the distinction many banks use: the product manager owns strategy, outcomes and the roadmap; the product owner translates that into a prioritized backlog and works daily with the agile team. Be honest about which you have done, with an example of each part, and how you would grow into the role on offer.

looking_for: Understanding of product roles at the firm
strong_signals: Link to the role on offer

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Delivers well-defined tasks within an agile team, with guidance; writes correct, tested code.
Owns features and services within a team, handles production support and can design components.
Leads design for a product area, mentors engineers and is accountable for reliability and controls.
Leads multiple teams or a platform, sets technical direction and manages senior stakeholders across a line of business.
Owns a backlog or a product feature set with a product lead's guidance.
Owns a product and its outcomes, manages stakeholders across business, technology and risk.
Leads a product portfolio and team of product managers; long tenure managing complex programs expected.

persona.pace: Brisk; Superday rounds are back to back and often mix technical and behavioral questions in one slot
persona.pushback_style: Asks 'what happens on a retry?', 'how would you prove that to an auditor?', 'who did you tell?' and expects calm, process-based answers
persona.closing_style: Leaves a few minutes for questions; recruiter follows up on next steps

case_style.notes: Engineering cases are banking systems with correctness, controls and audit at the centre. Product cases, where used, improve a banking or payments product within risk and regulatory limits. Market sizing is rare.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the four principles come from the official Business Principles page; the firm's longer document has around 20 sub-principles, which we folded into the four descriptions.

loop_structure: SWE loop from two prep guides plus Glassdoor reports; Superday format varies (two 30-minute to four 60-minute rounds). data_ml and pm loops are thin; the PM case round is reported only for some teams.

bar_by_level: SWE title-to-level mapping (SE II Analyst, SE III Associate, Lead SE VP, ED) comes from one prep site's compensation table; scope text is our summary. The Dataford PM page returned 429, so PM level expectations rest on its search snippet.
persona: inferred from prep-guide advice (calm, process-based answers, auditor framing); no official description.
scoring_weights: our estimate; accuracy and ownership raised for the bank's stress on controls and incidents.
case_style: few public reports of product cases at JPMorganChase.
